extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR and compliance officers, labor/employment lawyers, policymakers, and stakeholders submitting comments on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final-rule provisions from the FTC explaining which practices involving non-compete clauses constitute unfair methods of competition, how the Commission weighed evidence and comments, and how the rule treats existing agreements and senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entering into or attempting to enter into non-competes (§910.2(a)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a worker other than a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person to enter into or attempt to enter into a non-compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule adopts the proposed language prohibiting entering into or attempting to enter into non-competes with workers other than senior executives. The Commission explains that 'attempt to enter into' covers conduct such as presenting the worker with a non-compete even if not ultimately executed, because such attempts have in terrorem effects that deter competition (workers may refrain from seeking other work or starting a business). The Commission rejected removing the 'attempt' language despite commenters' concerns that it could encourage meritless suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcing or attempting to enforce non-competes (§910.2(a)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a worker other than a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prohibition targets future enforcement or attempted enforcement conduct taken after the effective date. An employer 'attempts to enforce' when it takes steps toward initiating legal action even if the court does not enter a final order. The Commission removed a proposed rescission requirement (i.e., employers need not formally rescind prior non-competes) to reduce employer burden and clarified the rule focuses on prospective enforcement conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing a worker is subject to a non-compete without a good-faith basis (§910.2(a)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an unfair method of competition for an employer to represent that a worker other than a senior executive is subject to a non-compete clause where the employer has no good faith basis to believe the worker is subject to an enforceable non-compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prong includes prohibitions on threatening to enforce a non-compete against a worker; advising a worker not to pursue a job opportunity because of a non-compete; or telling a worker they are subject to a non-compete. The final rule retains 'good faith' language but moves it to §910.3 (exceptions). The Commission rejects narrowing this prong to statements about validity under local or State law, because representing a worker is subject to a non-compete when the rule renders it unenforceable would mislead and deter workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: In terrorem effect—rationale for attempt and representation prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers' presentation of non-competes, threats to litigate, or representations that workers are subject to non-competes have in terrorem effects that deter workers from seeking or accepting work or starting businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission emphasizes that even unenforceable or unexecuted non-competes can chill worker mobility because workers may not realize they are not bound or cannot afford litigation. This underlies the rule's scope (attempts and representations) and supports prohibiting threats and informational misrepresentations even where the worker may believe the clause unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of existing non-competes for non-senior workers (no rescission requirement but no future enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For workers other than senior executives, the final rule does not require formal rescission but prohibits enforcement or attempted enforcement of existing non-competes after the effective date; existing non-competes thus will not remain in force insofar as they would be enforced after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission removed 'maintain' from the text to avoid implying a rescission obligation and to reduce employer burden. Instead employers must simply refrain from enforcement or attempted enforcement after the effective date. The Commission concluded existing non-competes with non-senior workers impose acute, ongoing harms and therefore should not remain in force after the effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior executive exception and special treatment (§910.2(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule treats non-competes with senior executives differently: it finds such non-competes restrictive and exclusionary conduct but allows existing non-competes with senior executives to remain in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission does not find senior executives are exploited or coerced to the same degree as other workers; they are more likely to have negotiated terms and received compensation. Because of practical concerns in untangling complex compensation arrangements, the rule permits existing senior-executive non-competes to remain enforceable while still recognizing those clauses as unfair methods of competition in the abstract. The rule includes a definition of 'senior executive' targeted at highly paid workers with the highest levels of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence weighting: empirical literature, comment record, and Commission expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission bases findings on the totality of evidence including review of empirical literature, the full comment record, and its expertise in identifying practices that harm competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where reliable empirical studies exist (e.g., Hausman and Lavetti on prices in healthcare), the Commission considers them; where empirical literature is lacking for some effects (e.g., product/service quality), the Commission accords weight to the voluminous public comments describing harms. Small-sample studies are given limited weight; a large number of consistent comments can bolster findings even when quantitative studies are scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary benefits to a firm do not justify unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that non-competes increase revenue, referrals, or wages for a firm does not justify the use of non-competes if they constitute an unfair method of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes that some studies show in-group referrals increase revenue, but such pecuniary benefits cannot justify practices that harm competition or patient care. The rule focuses on competitive harms rather than firms' short-term pecuniary gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of less burdensome alternatives to protect employer interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers have adequate alternatives to non-competes to protect trade secrets and retention interests, including trade secret law, nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), fixed-duration employment contracts, and competing on pay/benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds NDAs and trade secret law do not impose the same burden on competition as non-competes and notes that many employers who used non-competes also have NDAs. The rule does not prevent employers from entering new NDAs. For retention, employers may use fixed-duration contracts or improved compensation rather than non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of bargaining and compensation for non-senior workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non-competes with workers other than senior executives generally are not bargained for and such workers generally do not receive meaningful compensation in exchange for agreeing to non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding supports treating existing non-competes for non-senior workers as harmful and not allowing them to remain in force after the effective date; commenters' claims that invalidation would upset bargained-for agreements were not persuasive given the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement that employers recoup benefits paid for non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not adopt a mechanism requiring employers to recoup previously paid benefits given in exchange for non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised concerns about whether employers could recoup benefits already paid; the Commission addressed these concerns in the record but did not require recoupment as part of the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of enforcement prohibition is prospective (post-effective-date)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-senior workers, the prohibition on enforcing or attempting to enforce applies to enforcement conduct that occurs after the effective date; employers need not take affirmative steps to rescind prior contract provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach reduces burdens on employers and focuses the rule on future enforcement behavior rather than mandating retroactive contract rescission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt-to-enforce definition includes steps toward litigation even without final court order
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer 'attempts to enforce' a non-compete when it takes steps toward initiating legal action to enforce the non-compete, even if the court does not enter a final order enforcing the non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures that pre-litigation or litigation-threat conduct that would chill competition is covered by the enforcement prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission's reliance on comment volume and qualitative reports regarding product/service quality and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Where quantitative studies are limited, the Commission treats the large number of consistent public comments (especially from healthcare professionals) describing reduced product/service quality, reduced patient access, and healthcare shortages as corroborating evidence of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record includes hundreds of comments describing harms such as disrupted continuity of care, increased travel burdens, worse health outcomes, and provider shortages—especially in rural and underserved areas—and the Commission finds these qualitative reports bolster its findings despite limited empirical quantification.
